title: Current as rate of flow of charge (Q = It)
keyIdea: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: the number of coulombs that pass a point each second. So charge = current × time, Q = I t, with charge Q in coulombs (C), current I in amperes (A) and time t in seconds (s). A current of 1 A means 1 C passes each second. Rearranged, I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I. Convert minutes and hours to seconds and milliamps to amps before you use the equation. In a single series loop the current is the same at every point, because charge is not used up; a lamp transfers energy, not charge.
familyTip: Find the rating on a phone charger or a power bank, often written in mA or mAh. Ask: if the charger gives 2 A for one hour, how many coulombs flow? (2 × 3,600 = 7,200 C.) Then ask how long a 500 mA current would take to move the same charge.

visual.caption: Which of these let exactly 6 coulombs of charge pass? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: count charge through a gate, find the time for a fixed charge, beat the unit traps, draw charge–time lines, check the current round a loop.

kid: Current is how much charge flows past a point each second. We count charge in coulombs, C. We measure current in amps, A. One amp means one coulomb goes past each second.
So charge equals current times time: Q = I × t. Two amps for three seconds lets six coulombs pass. To find the time, flip it round: t = Q ÷ I. Half the current takes twice as long.
Time must be in seconds. Five minutes is 300 seconds, not 5. Current must be in amps. 200 mA is 0.2 A. Change the units first, then use the rule.
In one loop, the current is the same all the way round. A lamp does not use up charge. It takes energy from the charge as it flows through.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. AQA GCSE Physics (8463, 4.2.1.3) defines current as the rate of flow of electrical charge and requires Q = I t, with charge in coulombs, current in amperes and time in seconds; it also states that the current is the same at any point in a single closed loop. OCR Gateway and Edexcel specifications set the same equation. Key words: charge, coulomb, current, ampere, rate of flow, series circuit, milliamp.

In SI terms one coulomb is the charge carried by a current of 1 A in 1 s. The elementary charge is exactly 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so 1 C is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. On a charge–time graph a steady current gives a straight line through the origin whose gradient is the current.

The most common mistake is leaving time in minutes or hours, or current in milliamps, before substituting. Another is inverting the rearrangement, for example giving I = t ÷ Q. A persistent misconception is that current is used up by a lamp, so it is smaller after the lamp than before it.

In the lab your child sets a current so that 6 C passes a gate in 3 s, finds the currents that move 12 C in 4 s and in 8 s, answers three unit-trap questions, drags charge–time lines to slopes of 2 A and 3.5 A, and reads the current at four points round a series loop.

practice.prompt: A current of {a} A flows through a lamp for 5 minutes. How much charge passes, in coulombs?
practice.hint: Change 5 minutes to seconds first, then use Q = I × t.

practice.prompt: A charge of {a}0 C flows past a point in 5 s. What is the current, in amps?
practice.hint: Current is charge per second: I = Q ÷ t.

practice.prompt: A current of 250 mA flows for 40 s. How much charge passes?
practice.hint: Change milliamps to amps first: divide by 1,000.
practice.explain: 250 mA = 0.25 A. Q = 0.25 × 40 = 10 C. Using 250 gives 10,000 C, a thousand times too big.

practice.prompt: In a series circuit the ammeter before the lamp reads 0.6 A. What does an ammeter after the lamp read?
practice.hint: Is charge used up as it passes through the lamp?
practice.explain: Charge is not used up, so the current is the same at every point in a series loop: 0.6 A.

practice.prompt: How long does it take for 90 C to pass at a current of 3 A?
practice.hint: Rearrange Q = I t to find t.
practice.explain: t = Q ÷ I = 90 ÷ 3 = 30 s. Multiplying gives 270, which has the wrong units.

pool.prompt: A current of 2 A flows for {a} minutes. How much charge passes, in coulombs?
How many seconds does it take for {a}00 C to pass at a current of 4 A?
pool.hint: Rearrange Q = I t to get t = Q ÷ I, then divide.

pool.prompt: What does a current of 1 ampere mean?
choices: 1 coulomb of charge passes a point each second
1 coulomb of charge is used up each second
Each coulomb is given 1 joule of energy
pool.hint: Current is a rate of flow.
pool.explain: 1 A = 1 C per second. Energy per coulomb is potential difference, measured in volts.

pool.prompt: On a charge–time graph, line X is steeper than line Y. Which has the bigger current?
pool.explain: Gradient = Q ÷ t = I, so the steeper line X has the bigger current.

pool.prompt: A torch draws 400 mA for 30 minutes. How much charge passes?
pool.hint: Convert both: mA to A, minutes to seconds.
pool.explain: 0.4 A × 1,800 s = 720 C. 12 C forgets the minutes; 12,000 C forgets the milliamps.

pool.prompt: The current through a motor is halved. How long does the same charge now take to pass?
pool.hint: Keep Q fixed and use t = Q ÷ I: what happens when I gets smaller?
pool.explain: With Q fixed, t = Q ÷ I, so halving I doubles t.

pool.prompt: Mia says a lamp in a series loop 'uses up some of the current'. What is wrong with this?
choices: Charge is not used up; the current is the same all round
Nothing, the current drops after a lamp
pool.hint: What did the counting ring read at every point?
pool.explain: The same charge passes every point each second, so the current is the same all round. The lamp transfers energy from the charge to its surroundings.

pool.prompt: Which equation gives the current from the charge and the time?
pool.explain: Rearranging Q = I t gives I = Q ÷ t, which matches the unit C/s.
